title: Oxtail Soup
subtitle: A rich, slow-cooked British oxtail broth with root vegetables
excerpt: Oxtail pieces braised until the meat falls from the bone, then the cooking liquid is reduced to a deep, gelatinous soup. A Victorian British standard that takes time but almost no skill.
sourceNotes: Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), Project Gutenberg #10136. Oxtail soup is listed as a standard British dinner soup. Eliza Acton, Modern Cookery for Private Families (1845), ox-tail soup documented as a rich broth made from cheap cuts. Oxtail soup was widely sold as a commercial product by firms including Heinz and Baxter's from the late nineteenth century onwards.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the finished soup for up to 3 months. Reheat gently and stir before serving as the gelatin may cause it to set solid when cold.
recipe.batchNotes: Make a double batch in a large stock pot. The flavour improves over 2 to 3 days in the fridge.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The soup is significantly better made a day ahead: the fat rises and can be skimmed off cold, and the flavour deepens overnight.

content.text: Oxtail soup is not a light broth: it is a thick, gelatinous, deeply flavoured soup made by braising oxtail joints until the meat falls from the bone, then reducing the cooking liquid with root vegetables. The high collagen content of the tail joints gives the finished soup a lip-coating body that no stock cube can replicate. It takes three and a half hours but requires almost no active attention.

items.prepNote: cut into joints, trimmed of excess fat

content.text: Heat oven to 160 degrees C. Season {{oxtail}} of oxtail joints and dust with {{plain-flour}} of flour. Heat {{sunflower-oil}} of oil in a large casserole over high heat. Brown the oxtail pieces in batches until deep brown on all sides, 4 to 5 minutes per batch. Remove and set aside.
In the same pot, cook {{onion}}, {{carrot}}, and {{celery}} over medium heat for 5 minutes. Add {{garlic}} of garlic and {{tomato-puree}} of tomato puree. Stir for 2 minutes.

Return the oxtail to the pot. Add {{stock-beef}} of beef stock, {{bay-leaves}}, {{thyme-fresh}}, and {{worcestershire-sauce}} of Worcestershire sauce. Bring to a simmer, cover, and transfer to the oven. Braise for 3 hours until the meat is completely tender and falling from the bone.
Remove the oxtail with a slotted spoon. When cool enough to handle, pull the meat from the bones and shred it. Discard the bones and the herb sprigs.

Strain the cooking liquid through a sieve, pressing the vegetables. Discard the solids. Return the liquid and shredded meat to the pot. If the soup is too thin, simmer uncovered for 15 to 20 minutes to concentrate it. Season well and serve with crusty bread.

rows.symptom: Soup is thin and watery with no body
rows.cause: Not enough oxtail relative to the liquid, or cooked too quickly
rows.fix: Use at least 1.2 kg of oxtail for 6 servings. The gelatin in the joints dissolves slowly at a low, steady temperature. If the soup is thin after straining, reduce it uncovered on the hob.

rows.cause: Oxtail not trimmed or soup not skimmed
rows.fix: Trim the excess fat from the oxtail before browning. Make the soup a day ahead, refrigerate, and lift the solidified fat from the surface before reheating.

rows.cause: Temperature too low, or pieces too large
rows.fix: Check the oven temperature is correct. The liquid should be at a gentle simmer throughout, not a cold steep. Oxtail can take up to 4 hours in some ovens.

rows.cause: Oxtail not browned well enough at the start
rows.fix: The browning step adds the majority of the deep, savoury flavour. Do it in batches over high heat, not all at once in a crowded pan, and do not rush it.

content.text: Oxtail soup was a staple of Victorian and Edwardian British cooking. It appeared on the dinner menus of country houses and working-class households alike. The cheap, collagen-rich joints suited long, slow cooking. By the twentieth century, canned versions made the soup widely available. The fresh, home-braised version is much more flavourful than the tinned product. It is now found on winter restaurant menus and in British food writing focused on revived traditional dishes.
